clue.text: Don't keep us in the dark: it's Earth

definitions.text: Don't keep us in the dark

definitions.meaning: The Roman goddess of the earth, and a poetic name for the planet

explanation.surface: Someone begs to be let in on a secret, which turns out to be the name of our planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tellus is the Latin and mythological personification of the planet, so it names our world.

clue.text: Message about ruler to go up: no 37.5p licence fee was needed

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the message wraps round the ruler

parts.note: word means a message, as in 'send word'
a king is a ruler

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word go is written bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A note about the monarch going up the hierarchy, followed by a remark about dog licences.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain's dog licence cost 37½p until it was abolished in 1987; working dogs such as sheepdogs and guide dogs were exempt from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Working animals such as farm collies were exempt from the old British dog licence, so the description fits them.

clue.text: Equivocator gets change through being put out

indicators.note: put out in the sense of extended or spread round, so the word for through wraps the change

parts.note: per means through or by means of
to alter is to change

explanation.surface: A shifty speaker gets annoyed by being changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being put out' looks like annoyance; here it means stretched out, the word for through extended round the change.
explanation.definitionFit: To palter is to talk evasively or shift ground, so one who does so equivocates.

clue.text: 18's venerable Ulsterman getting on amid artistic nihilism

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so the other pieces are placed inside the art movement

parts.note: Dada was the anti-art, nihilistic artistic movement of the early twentieth century
NI is short for Northern Ireland, the bulk of Ulster
an elder is a venerable senior person, as in church elders
on as in 'getting on', advancing

explanation.surface: An elderly Northern Irishman ageing in the midst of a nihilist art movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is GEORGE ELIOT, and this is one of her novels. Ulster churches have elders, which helps the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Deronda is the last novel written by George Eliot, the author in clue 18.

clue.text: The Queen is in the joint, scoffing

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the queen and the verb sit within the joint

parts.note: a dive is a seedy bar or joint
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
taken as written

explanation.surface: The monarch is found eating greedily in a low dive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scoffing' looks like eating greedily; here it means mocking.
explanation.definitionFit: Derisive means mocking, which is what scoffing is.

clue.text: Unidentified beast with no head in place of monster

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the shortened beast sits within the place

parts.note: Loch Ness in Scotland is home of the legendary monster

indicators.note: with no head means the first letter of the beast is removed

parts.note: a camel is a beast of burden

explanation.surface: An unknown headless creature lurks where a monster lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unidentified has no name given to it, so it lacks a label.

clue.text: Report of eyeglass belonging to monk

indicators.note: a report is a sound, so the word for the eyeglass is spoken

parts.note: a monocle is a single eyeglass

explanation.surface: Gossip about a single lens owned by a monk.
explanation.definitionFit: Monachal is the adjective for monks and monastic life.

clue.text: 18's so-called happy man at home on the river

definitions.meaning: Felix ..., the Radical is a George Eliot novel, and the Latin name Felix means happy
an otter's den on a riverbank

explanation.surface: A cheerful man from a Victorian novel lives by the water.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of Eliot's hero Felix is also the word for an otter's riverside lair.

clue.text: Sad end of 18's workplace on the river

definitions.text: Sad end of 18's workplace on the river

indicators.note: end of means only the closing letters of the novel title are kept

parts.note: The Mill on the Floss is George Eliot's novel named after a mill on the river Floss

explanation.surface: The unhappy close of a novelist's riverside mill story.
explanation.walkthrough: The last four letters of 'Mill on the Floss' give the answer, and the novel does end sadly, with brother and sister drowned in a flood.
explanation.definitionFit: The bereavement that closes the novel is a sad ending, a loss of life.

clue.text: 18's gold-backed tooth (detail)

indicators.note: backed means turned back to front, so gold is read in reverse

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold

indicators.note: detail means removing the tail, the last letter of the tooth

parts.note: a molar is a back tooth

explanation.surface: A novelist's gold tooth, described in detail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detail' looks like close description; it means cut off the tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Romola is George Eliot's historical novel set in Renaissance Florence.

clue.text: Burlesque with outlets for game

annotationWithheld.why: Burlesque with outlets for game (8): SKIT gives the start, but TLES can come only from 'outlets' read as 'lets' shuffled by 'out', one word acting as fodder and indicator at once

clue.text: 18's sailor's first off — first sails off

indicators.note: first says the shuffled sails come before the other piece
off means out of order, so the letters of sails are rearranged
first off means the first i of the sailor's word is dropped

parts.note: a mariner is a sailor; the possessive adds nothing

explanation.surface: A sailor's lead is lost, then the leading sails come off.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the first I from MARINER to get MARNER; rearrange SAILS to SILAS, placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: Silas Marner is George Eliot's novel about a reclusive weaver.

clue.text: In Welsh mouths, not English, second people on the run

indicators.note: not means the letter for English is removed
in means placed inside, so second goes within the Welsh word

parts.note: aber is Welsh for a river mouth, as in Aberystwyth
taken as written

explanation.surface: In Welsh speech the English vanish, and those who second a motion run off.
explanation.walkthrough: Aber, Welsh for a river mouth, begins place names like Aberystwyth; the first E of the combination is the one dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Absconders are those who have fled, typically from custody, so they are on the run.

clue.text: One French and several German children are not so gentle

parts.note: un is French for one
Kinder is German for children

explanation.surface: A French child and some German ones prove rough.
explanation.definitionFit: Unkinder is the comparative of unkind, meaning less gentle.

clue.text: Norman style leader

parts.note: not architecture from 1066 but a fashion leader whose first name was Norman, the Queen's dressmaker

explanation.surface: A leader of Norman architecture.
explanation.walkthrough: Norman Hartnell was the British couturier who designed Elizabeth II's coronation gown.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Norman Hartnell was the leading British fashion designer of his day, a true leader of style.

clue.text: 6's bird's opposite number

parts.note: six is VI in Roman numerals, plus the S of the possessive
avis is Latin for bird; the possessive adds nothing

explanation.surface: A bird belonging to the monk in clue 6 faces its counterpart.
explanation.walkthrough: '6' looks like a cross-reference to clue 6; it is the Roman numeral VI.
explanation.definitionFit: A vis-a-vis is a person in a corresponding position, a counterpart.

clue.text: Nurse goes round African country, being of no fixed abode

indicators.note: goes round means encircles, so the nurse wraps the country

parts.note: a VAD was a nurse of the Voluntary Aid Detachment
Gabon is a country in West Africa

explanation.surface: A nurse travels around Africa with no settled home.
explanation.walkthrough: A VAD was a volunteer nurse in Britain in the two World Wars.
explanation.definitionFit: A vagabond wanders without a settled home, used adjectivally here.

clue.text: See 4
Earth or horse? (Reactionary Labour writer)

parts.note: Ge or Gaia is the Greek earth goddess
taken as written
gee, or gee-gee, is a child's word for horse

indicators.note: reactionary means going backwards, so labour is read in reverse

parts.note: toil is labour

explanation.surface: A question about earth or horse, with a backward-looking Labour author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the British political party; it is just work.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, the Victorian novelist.

clue.text: You need to ride craftily to manage a title

indicators.note: craftily means artfully, so the letters of to ride are reworked

explanation.surface: You have to ride cleverly to win a championship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'title' looks like a sporting championship; it is a magazine or newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: An editor is the person who runs a publication, called a title in the trade.

clue.text: French boy for Mother Church?

parts.note: ma is mother
RC stands for Roman Catholic, a church

explanation.surface: A French lad stands in for Mother Church.
explanation.definitionFit: Marc is a common French boy's name, the equivalent of Mark.

clue.text: Vocation in 18's scenic book

indicators.note: in says the answer is found inside the book title, the letters either side being dropped

parts.note: Scenes of Clerical Life was George Eliot's first book

explanation.surface: A calling found in a novelist's picturesque volume.
explanation.walkthrough: The book is Scenes of Clerical Life; the answer runs across 'cleriCAL Life', so the letters on either side are discarded.
explanation.definitionFit: A call is a vocation, a sense of being summoned to a role.

clue.text: 18's first lady outside the border

parts.note: A is the first letter, as in grade A

indicators.note: outside means the lady wraps round the border

parts.note: a dame is a titled lady
a bed is a flower border

explanation.surface: A novelist's first lady stands outside the frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'border' looks like a frontier; it is a garden flower bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Bede was George Eliot's first full-length novel.

clue.text: 18's heart needing 20 hearts

indicators.note: needing means lacking, so pieces are taken away from the novel

parts.note: Middlemarch is George Eliot's best-known novel
the answer to clue 20 is a French boy's name
H is the abbreviation for hearts in card games

explanation.surface: A novelist's central part needs twenty hearts.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the answer to 20 plus H from Middlemarch leaves the first part of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The middle of something is its heart or centre.

clue.text: Copper under training in a line from the kitchen

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
L is a learner, someone under training
taken as written
RY stands for railway, a line

explanation.surface: A policeman in training stands in line in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman; it is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Culinary means having to do with cooking and the kitchen.

clue.text: Plant or horse for 22

definitions.meaning: a leafy herb with a sour taste
Hetty, the dairymaid in Adam Bede, has this surname

explanation.surface: A plant or a horse to suit a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorrel is a sour-leaved herb, a chestnut horse, and Hetty's surname in Eliot's novel.
